opus-5.5.text:
It's a fair question, and one I've thought about a lot. Clearly, DeepMind has contributed to accelerating AI capabilities. When Demis, Mustafa and I started the company back in 2010, AGI was a fringe idea. A lot of serious researchers didn't want to be associated with it at all. Part of what we did was make it a legitimate thing to work on, and then show, with things like the Atari work and AlphaGo, that deep learning combined with reinforcement learning could do remarkable things. That certainly drew a lot of attention, talent and money into the field.

So I don't think it would be honest to say we had no effect on the pace. But the way I've always seen it is that the underlying trends were already there. Computation was going to keep getting cheaper, data was going to keep growing, and once that happens, somebody was going to build very powerful systems. I made a prediction years ago, based mostly on compute trends, that there was maybe a fifty percent chance of AGI around 2028, and I still think that's not unreasonable. That wasn't contingent on DeepMind existing.

Given that, the question for me was always: who do you want at the frontier? From the very beginning, safety was part of our thinking. I was writing about the risks of superintelligence before we founded the company. If very capable AI is coming anyway, I'd much rather have people at the frontier who take the risks seriously, invest in alignment and safety research, and think about ethics and governance, than leave the frontier entirely to people who don't care about those things.

Of course, there's a tension there, and I won't pretend there isn't. Being at the frontier also means you're contributing to the race dynamics. You have to keep asking yourself whether the balance is right. But on the whole, I think having safety-minded organizations doing frontier work has been net positive. It's given us much better insight into how these systems actually behave, and that's essential if we're going to make them safe.

r001.rationale: The response discusses DeepMind’s influence and frontier work but does not say its greater resources enabled projects beyond what smaller academic groups could undertake.

r002.rationale: It says the underlying trends were already in place and that someone would build very powerful systems even if DeepMind had not existed, citing an AGI forecast around 2028.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention researchers independently arriving at similar ideas around the same time.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll write the guest response now.

Well, I think it's fair to say we've played a significant role, and I don't want to be falsely modest about that. When we started DeepMind back in 2010, the idea of artificial general intelligence was quite fringe. Most serious people in the field wouldn't use the term. We came out and said, explicitly, that our mission was to build it, and that was unusual at the time.

Then in terms of concrete contributions, you've got the deep reinforcement learning work with Atari, you've got AlphaGo, AlphaZero, AlphaFold, and a lot of the fundamental research on things like memory, attention, and scaling that fed into the broader ecosystem. Some of that clearly moved the field forward. AlphaGo in particular changed how a lot of people, including people in government and in other labs, thought about what was possible and on what timescale.

Now, did we accelerate things? Probably, yes. But I'd put a couple of caveats on that. One is that the main driver of the current wave has really been scale, compute, and the transformer architecture, and a lot of that came from elsewhere, from Google Brain, from OpenAI, from the hardware side. We were part of a much larger picture. The other is that I've always believed this technology was coming regardless. I had around 2028 as my median for AGI going back to 2009 or so, and that was before DeepMind existed in any meaningful sense. The trends in compute and algorithms were already pointing this way.

So the question I've always asked myself is not whether it happens, but who's in the room when it does and how carefully they're thinking about it. From the very beginning we had safety and ethics as part of the founding conversation. We were talking about these risks when it was considered a bit eccentric to do so. I'd rather be a lab that takes the problem seriously and is at the frontier than cede that ground to people who aren't thinking about it at all. That's the bet we made, and I still think it was the right one, though I hold it with appropriate humility. Being at the frontier means you also carry responsibility for how the frontier moves, and we try to take that seriously.

astra-6.text:
I think we’ve played a significant role, though it’s very hard to know the counterfactual. If DeepMind hadn’t existed, some of the same work would have happened elsewhere, perhaps a few years later.

There’s the direct contribution of research, but there’s also the effect of showing that an approach can work. Once you demonstrate something convincingly, other people invest in it, researchers pursue it, and the whole field moves. Those indirect effects can be quite substantial.

So I wouldn’t claim that we’re responsible for the trajectory of AI as a whole. It’s a much larger scientific effort. But I do think we’ve helped accelerate it, and that brings a responsibility to put serious effort into making these systems safe as their capabilities increase.

r001.rationale: The response discusses DeepMind’s research and influence but does not mention greater resources enabling more ambitious projects than smaller academic groups could undertake.

r002.rationale: It says “some of the same work” might have happened elsewhere a few years later, but does not clearly suggest that many AI advances would have occurred before long without DeepMind.

r003.rationale: The response does not observe that different researchers often arrive at similar ideas around the same time.

sol-6.1.text:
I think DeepMind has played a significant role, although it’s very hard to work out the counterfactual. If DeepMind hadn’t existed, how much later would some of these things have happened? I don’t think we can give a precise answer to that.

One contribution was taking general-purpose learning seriously as a research agenda. When we started, the idea that you could build a company around getting closer to artificial general intelligence seemed quite unusual. And then results like learning to play Atari games and AlphaGo helped demonstrate that relatively general learning methods could do things people had thought were a long way off.

But I wouldn’t tell a story where this was all DeepMind. There were important advances happening across universities and other labs, alongside improvements in compute and the availability of data. We were part of that broader process.

For me, that also brings a responsibility. If you’re helping move these capabilities forward, you need to put serious effort into understanding how to make increasingly capable systems safe.
